title: Containers, iterators and algorithms
objectives: Use vector capacity/size and iterator invalidation rules to mutate/erase safely without retaining invalid element/end observers.
Choose an order/duplicate-preserving representation and apply a strict-order stable algorithm without silently changing identity, tie or caller-mutation policy.
Apply containers, iterators and algorithms invariants safely and identify scope boundaries.
motivation: Choose a container from the data contract before guessing at speed. An ordinary std::vector<T> (excluding the specialized vector<bool>) is a contiguous dynamic sequence that preserves order and repeated values; it is a natural starting point for a small replay/snapshot sequence.

blocks.md: Choose a container from the data contract before guessing at speed. An ordinary std::vector<T> (excluding the specialized vector<bool>) is a contiguous dynamic sequence that preserves order and repeated values; it is a natural starting point for a small replay/snapshot sequence. A unique-key associative map stores at most one value per key, so a construction/assignment keyed only by a repeated trade label can lose multiplicity. A set represents uniqueness, not a counted event log. Stable business identity and chronological ordering are separate metadata, not properties inferred from a container type. This lesson uses synthetic labels, not authenticated execution IDs.

vector.size() counts constructed elements; capacity() counts storage available before growth requires reallocation. reserve(n) may increase capacity but does not create elements or change size. Indexing a reserved-but-unconstructed slot is not made valid by capacity. For this lesson, use at(i) for checked element access; an out-of-range access raises std::out_of_range rather than supplying a valid missing value. Do not read or write end(): it is a one-past position, not an element.

An iterator is a position/access mechanism under a container-specific validity contract, not a permanent business identifier. For vector, capacity-changing reserve invalidates all element iterators/references/pointers and end(); reserve without capacity change does not. push_back with reallocation invalidates all; without reallocation it still invalidates the old end(). erase invalidates the erased position and everything at/after it, including end(). Sorting can permute values even if storage remains, so a still-dereferenceable slot need not denote the same business record. Reacquire positions from current valid state; do not probe an invalid old iterator to see whether the bytes survived.

blocks.title: Erase without stepping through an invalid iterator
items: Start [1,2,3,4] at begin(). Keep 1 and increment. On 2, erase returns the next valid position now holding 3; assign that return to it, without incrementing the invalid old iterator.
Keep 3 and increment. On 4, erase returns the updated end(); the next condition ends the loop. Survivors [1,3] keep their original order.
A naive erase(it); ++it uses an invalidated iterator and can skip values or have undefined behavior. This explanation does not execute that invalid program.

blocks.caption: Expected output: 2, 2, 3, 1, 3, 5 on separate lines. After removal size is 2; reserve(16) leaves it 2. at(1) reacquires the current second value 3. Adding 5 then iterating current begin/end is safe. No address/capacity growth factor or stale-iterator behavior is assumed.

blocks.md: The explicit single-erase loop makes validity easy to trace, but repeated vector erases can shift many elements and cost quadratic time in total. For bulk filtering, erase-remove or C++20 std::erase_if can compact once under their contracts. Do not claim all vector operations are constant time: element access is constant time, end insertion is amortized constant time, and arbitrary middle erase/insertion shifts elements. reserve can reduce reallocations when a useful bound is known, but reserving exact next size before every append can defeat geometric growth. Measure realistic use rather than swapping containers on slogans.

Algorithms require more than a compilable callable. Sorting comparison must define a strict weak ordering: a<a is false; if a<b then not b<a; ordered comparisons and equivalence classes must be consistent/transitive. The integer price comparator below uses <, not <=. Equal-price elements are equivalent under that comparator. stable_sort preserves their original relative order; std::sort does not promise that tie preservation. Stability is a declared snapshot policy, not a claim that a venue uses price-time priority or that a repeated label is a retried fill.

blocks.caption: Expected lines: T2:10, T1:10, T1:20, T1:20, 3. The first three lines are the stable sorted copy; equal-price T2 precedes the later T1. The fourth confirms the original first record is unchanged. All 3 records survive, including repeated labels. No map overwrite, deduplication, live book or execution guarantee is implied.

blocks.md: Do not retain raw element pointers across mutations unless the exact operation/type contract proves them valid. Node-based and hash containers have different iterator/reference rules, ordering guarantees, memory costs and performance profiles; choose/read those contracts before substituting one. For persistence or parallel mutation, synchronization, versioned identity and durable replay are additional requirements. This lesson is a single-threaded in-memory demonstration.

Independent transfer: filter a vector with no matches, all matches and adjacent even values, checking survivor order and size. Replace the repeated-erase implementation with C++20 std::erase_if and compare outputs, without dereferencing stale iterators. Sort a snapshot with many equal prices and repeated labels, proving multiplicity, stable ties, sortedness and original immutability separately. Explain why changing < to <= violates the comparator contract even if one small run appears sorted.

Sources: [vector contracts](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/container/vector.html), [erase and returned iterator](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/container/vector/erase.html), [reserve](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/container/vector/reserve.html), and [stable_sort](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/algorithm/stable_sort.html). Ordinary successful single-threaded operations are used; allocation/throwing element operations and other containers need their own reviewed exception/validity contracts.

guidedExercise.prompt: A stored vector iterator still prints a plausible value after reallocation. What should a review say?
hints: Uses documented invalidation rather than lucky bytes.
Separates business identity from an iterator slot.
Proposes reacquisition without executing invalid access.
guidedExercise.solution: Do not use that output as validity evidence. Capacity-changing vector operations invalidate prior element observers, and later dereference can have undefined behavior. Reacquire valid state using current storage and stable business identity; do not run the invalid trace as a correctness test.

independentExercise.prompt: Write a small test case that deliberately breaks the contract boundary in "Containers, iterators and algorithms" and verify how your implementation rejects or handles it.
hints: Test zero, negative, empty, duplicate, and boundary values.
Confirm both time/memory complexity and numerical precision remain within spec.

commonMistakes: Storage capacity does not create live elements; access must remain within size. (Only existing element indices are valid.)
erase returns the next valid iterator or updated end, so the loop can continue without using the invalid old iterator. (The old erased position is invalidated.)
The survivors are [1,3], and reserve does not add constructed elements.

summary: Containers carry ordering, duplication, mutation and invalidation contracts.
Preserve identity/multiplicity, reacquire valid vector positions after mutation, and use a strict-order comparator with an explicit tie policy rather than trusting a plausible sorted output.

quiz.prompt: What does values.reserve(16) establish for a vector whose size is 2?
options: There are now 16 constructed values ready to index
The old end iterator can always be dereferenced
Capacity is at least 16; size remains 2
All future appends are forever guaranteed not to reallocate
quiz.explanation: Storage capacity does not create live elements; access must remain within size. (Only existing element indices are valid.)

quiz.prompt: After erasing a vector element while looping, which step follows the shown safe pattern?
options: Assign the returned next iterator to it
Increment the erased old iterator first
Dereference the old end to find the final record
Assume erased bytes define a lasting record ID
quiz.explanation: erase returns the next valid iterator or updated end, so the loop can continue without using the invalid old iterator. (The old erased position is invalidated.)

quiz.prompt: After removing even values from [1,2,3,4] and then reserve(16), what is the vector size?
quiz.explanation: The survivors are [1,3], and reserve does not add constructed elements.

quiz.prompt: Why use a vector for this synthetic event sequence with repeated labels?
options: It guarantees that each label occurs only once
Every repeated label is safely discarded
All operations are worst-case constant time
It preserves the sequence and repeated records
quiz.explanation: A unique-key map can silently collapse labels if used as a replay log without an explicit duplicate contract. (Duplicate meaning still needs a separate event policy.)

quiz.prompt: Why use price<other.price rather than price<=other.price for sorting?
options: Equal prices must be deleted before any sort
quiz.explanation: For integer keys, < satisfies the ordering structure; <= violates irreflexivity and the comparison requirements. (An item must not compare before itself.)
